title: Pattern darning
subtitle: Counted rows of running stitch worked in sequence to build geometric surface patterns
excerpt: Pattern darning is a counted-thread technique that uses rows of running stitch to build geometric patterns on the fabric surface. The needle passes over and under the weave of an evenweave fabric at counted intervals, with each row offset from the last to create a repeating pattern. It is one of the oldest filling methods in embroidery, found across many world traditions.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), darning stitch chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), darning stitch entry. Pattern darning is documented across European, Asian, and North African needlework traditions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fabric woven with the same thread count in both the horizontal and vertical directions, so that counting threads gives reliable stitch intervals in any direction.

content.text: Pattern darning builds a geometric surface pattern from nothing more than rows of running stitch counted across an

fabric. Each row passes over a set number of threads and under a set number, and the starting position of each row is offset from the one before. The pattern emerges from the offset alone, with no transfers or complex counting charts needed for simple repeats. It is an excellent introduction to counted embroidery and can be worked in a single colour or in several.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 to 4 strands; perle 8 for a bolder pattern

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Evenweave linen or Aida cloth; the weave must be clearly countable

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry needle size 24 or 26 (blunt) to pass between fabric threads without splitting them

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 20 cm embroidery hoop or a small frame

content.text: Choose a simple repeat, such as over 4 threads, under 2 threads. Bring the thread up at point (A) at the left edge of the area being filled. Pass the needle over 4 fabric threads and under 2, repeating across the row to point (B) at the right edge. Take the thread down.

Bring the thread up at the left edge again, 2 fabric threads below the first row. Work the same over-4-under-2 sequence, but begin 2 threads to the right of where the first row started. This offset shifts the pattern.
Work the third row 2 threads below the second, with the pattern start shifted by another 2 threads to the right. Continue this sequence until you complete one full pattern repeat.

Begin the next repeat below, returning the offset to the starting position. Fill the shape row by row. Fasten off at the back at the end of each thread, keeping the back neat so carried threads do not show through sheer fabrics.

items.symptom: The pattern repeat breaks or misaligns
items.cause: The count per row was not consistent, or the row spacing was uneven.
items.fix: Count carefully on every row before pulling the thread through. If the count is lost, pull back to the last correct row and recount from there.

items.symptom: The running stitches split the fabric threads rather than passing between them
items.fix: Use a blunt tapestry needle throughout. It slides between fabric threads cleanly and makes it easier to count the intervals.

items.symptom: The surface stitches on different rows are not the same length
items.cause: The offset was applied inconsistently, or a different over-under count was used on some rows.
items.fix: Write down the repeat sequence before starting: for example, over 4 / under 2 / offset by 2. Check the sequence at the start of each row.
